Start with the time course 🧭

For this lecture, the fastest way to answer a question is usually:

1. Time course→ 2. Exposure / symptom pattern→ 3. Objective inflammation?→ 4. Complication?→ 5. Treatment logic
Professor emphasis: “Time course is one of the most powerful diagnostic tools in rhinology.” Viral disease is usually under 10 days and improving; ABRS persists ≥10 days or “double worsens”; CRS lasts ≥12 weeks and requires objective inflammation.
<10 days, improving
Think viral rhinosinusitis → symptomatic care, no routine antibiotics.
≥10 days / double worsening
Think acute bacterial rhinosinusitis.
>4 discrete ABRS episodes/yr
Think RARS if symptom-free between episodes.
≥90 days / ≥12 weeks
Think CRS only if objective endoscopic/CT inflammation is present.

High-yield “don’t miss” list

  • OMC = frontal + maxillary + anterior ethmoid
  • Allergic rhinitis = type I, IgE-mediated
  • Spray away from septum → lateral wall
  • Topical decongestants >3 days → rebound congestion
  • Complicated sinusitis → cranial nerve exam + imaging
  • CRS = inflammatory, not just chronic infection
  • Surgery improves drainage/topical access; it does not “cure” inflammation

Normal anatomy you need before pathology

Nose functions

  • Filters + humidifies inspired air
  • Regulates airway resistance via turbinates and mucosal swelling
  • Environmental sensing: olfaction + trigeminal/general sensation
  • Innate + adaptive immune activity at an early environmental interface

Drainage map

RegionLecture drainage
Middle turbinate / OMCFrontal + maxillary + anterior ethmoid
Posterior / beneath superior turbinatePosterior ethmoid + sphenoid
Inferior meatusNasolacrimal duct
Why OMC matters: a shared narrow drainage pathway means pathology in one component can impair drainage of the connected frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses.

Selectable mechanism explorer

Predict the consequence

Why does chronic nasal inflammation cause obstruction?

Inflamed mucosa and turbinates swell, narrowing the airway and sinus ostia. With continued exposure, late-phase inflammation can make blockage the dominant symptom even when itching/sneezing are less obvious.

Why does ostial obstruction make sinus disease self-sustaining?

Mucus is still produced. If the drainage pathway narrows, mucus clearance falls → stasis → more inflammatory burden / microbial changes → more edema → further obstruction.

Why can CRS reduce smell?

Inflammation and/or polyps obstruct odorant access to the olfactory region, so odorants cannot effectively reach and bind olfactory receptors.

Why can allergies cause ear fullness?

The eustachian tube opens in the back of the nose. Nasal inflammation around that opening impairs middle-ear pressure equalization.

Sinusitis + Allergic Rhinitis Exam Sheet

Sinusitis + Allergic Rhinitis — Exam Sheet

1) Time course = first discriminator

  • Viral ARS: usually <10 d, not worsening → supportive care; no routine antibiotics or imaging.
  • ABRS: persistent ≥10 d without improvement or double worsening.
  • RARS: lecture slide: >4 discrete ABRS episodes/year, symptom-free between.
  • CRS: ≥90 continuous days / ≥12 wk + objective endoscopic/CT inflammation.

2) Drainage anatomy

  • OMC: frontal + maxillary + anterior ethmoid.
  • Posterior pathway: posterior ethmoid + sphenoid.
  • Inferior meatus: nasolacrimal duct.
  • Sphenoid neighbors: optic nerve, internal carotid, cavernous sinus / CNs.

3) Allergic rhinitis

Allergen → APC → Th2 → IL-4/IL-13 → B-cell class switch → IgE → FcεRI mast-cell priming → re-exposure/cross-link → degranulation → histamine.

  • Early: itch, sneeze, rhinorrhea, watery eyes.
  • Late: sustained congestion/blockage.
  • Testing must fit symptoms/exposure; positive IgE alone = sensitization, not necessarily clinical allergy.
  • Tx: allergen reduction + saline → intranasal steroid ± 2nd-gen antihistamine → intranasal antihistamine ± LTRA → immunotherapy selected patients.
  • Spray away from septum, toward lateral wall.
  • Topical decongestant >3 d → rhinitis medicamentosa.

4) Acute sinusitis

  • ARS: up to 4 wk of purulent drainage + obstruction and/or facial pain/pressure.
  • ABRS first-line: amoxicillin ± clavulanate 5–10 d (lecture).
  • Common organisms: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, S. pyogenes.
  • S. aureus: chronic disease/healthcare exposure; Pseudomonas: immunocompromised.

5) Complicated sinusitis

Orbit / brain / soft tissue / bone involvement → cranial nerve exam + imaging. Chandler progression discussed: periorbital cellulitis → orbital cellulitis → subperiosteal abscess → orbital abscess → cavernous sinus thrombosis.

6) CRS core concept

Barrier dysfunction + immune inflammation → mucosal edema/ostial obstruction → impaired mucociliary clearance → microbial community changes → more inflammation.

Exam trap: CRS is primarily inflammatory, not simply a chronic bacterial infection.

7) CRS treatment

  • Cornerstone: saline irrigation + intranasal corticosteroid.
  • Short oral steroid: selected CRSwNP.
  • Antibiotics: selective, not routine long-term therapy.
  • FESS: refractory disease; improves drainage, ventilation, and topical delivery.
  • Surgery does not cure allergy/inflammation/CF.

8) Biologics in CRSwNP

  • Omalizumab → anti-IgE
  • Dupilumab → anti-IL-4/13
  • Mepolizumab → anti-IL-5
  • Tezepelumab → anti-TSLP

9) Professor-question traps

  • OMC question: sphenoid is NOT included.
  • Orbital complication: include cranial nerve testing.
  • Professor polyp case answer key = surgical removal; note lecture’s broader treatment ladder still starts with topical anti-inflammatory therapy and reserves FESS for medically refractory disease.

Source nuances

Professor polyp question vs general CRS treatment ladder

The supplied practice key marks surgical removal of polyps for the 6-month obstructive/anosmia case. The lecture treatment slide separately describes saline + intranasal corticosteroid as first-line and surgery for medically refractory disease. The practice item is preserved exactly as keyed, and the distinction is called out after submission.

RARS threshold wording

Slide 35 says “>4 discrete episodes of ABRS per year”; the transcript also verbally says “more than 4.” This guide preserves the lecture wording rather than substituting an outside threshold.

“Five paired paranasal sinuses” wording

The deck counts anterior and posterior ethmoid sinuses as separate paired categories: frontal, maxillary, anterior ethmoid, posterior ethmoid, and sphenoid. This guide follows that lecture organization.
